newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian aluminium head says sector integration key.
newsitem.headline: Russian aluminium head says sector integration key.

text.p: The head of Russia's Kontsern Alyuminiy aluminium producers' group said on Friday domestic smelters had shown good production results but poorer financial returns in recent years and called for restructuring.
"Russia's aluminium sector is on the verge of crisis -- we need measures to remain competitive," said Igor Prokopov, the group's executive chairman, at a metallurgy news conference.
"We're barely competitive on world markets. Our production costs are higher than virtually anywhere else in the world."
He called for work with transnational commodities and other firms to continue and for vertical integration, including closer ties, possibly on the equity level, with electricity plants.

Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov has stepped up a probe of alleged crimes in Russia's aluminium sector, upsetting London-based Trans-World Group, which is working with Russian smelters but says it is is the target of unfair charges.
Prokopov repeated earlier statements that he saw some positive and some negative elements in Kulikov's investigation, but was hesitant to be more specific.
While he said restructuring as a whole was a task for smelters' shareholders (as opposed to the government), "a lot depended on the state".
"It's worth noting that shareholders have preserved (export) contacts and output," he said.
Trans-World, Glencore AG of Switzerland and Daewoo Corp of South Korea are among the major foreign shareholders at Russian smelters.

Prokopov said he wanted to see per capita domestic consumption of aluminium rise to 10-15 kg from three, but a metallurgical research specialist told the same conference this was unlikely given Russia's overall industrial decline.

Prokopov blamed smelters' financial woes on five-digit increases in energy and transport tariffs since 1991, problems in recouping a 20 percent value-added tax and high taxes, which he said consumed money needed for investment and modernisation.
"We want not privileges but fair energy tariffs and the right to conclude long-term contracts for energy and rail transport," he said.
Russian primary aluminium exports last year were the world's largest at 2.44 million tonnes out of total domestic output of 2.87 million tonnes.
